Content:
Recall that the inscribed angle theorem tells us that the measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of the central angle that intercepts the same arc.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/00a90207630535a5df1a4b6aa8246121]

Content:
We can use this theorem to solve different types of problems involving circles.

Content:
For instance, how can we find [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{UV}] in the diagram below?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d37a294d713b44c1e80198ae0d8059d1]

Content:
By considering the sum of the interior angles in [MATH: \triangle UVW], we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: m∠U + m∠V + m∠W|= 180^{∘}; 55^{∘} + 40^{∘} + m∠W|= 180^{∘}; 95^{∘} + m∠W|= 180^{∘}; m∠W|= 85^{∘}]

Content:
Now, according to the inscribed angle theorem, the measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7c251fcd580e72631866f3c0432de381]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: mUV^(⌢)|= 2m∠W; = 2 ⋅ 85^{∘}; = 170^{∘}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
According to the inscribed angle theorem, the measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc. [MATH: m∠P|= (1)/(2)mAB^(⌢); = (1)/(2) ⋅ 64^{∘}; = 32^{∘}.]

Therefore, by considering the sum of the interior angles in [MATH: \triangle ABP], we get the following:

[MATH: m∠A + m∠B + m∠P|= 180^{∘}; m∠A + 73^{∘} + 32^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠A + 105^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠A|= 75^{∘}]

sections.normalized_html: Given the picture below, find [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{BC}.]

Given the picture below, find [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{BC}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we will find [MATH: m\overset{\frown}{CDA}.]

The measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc. So, [MATH: mCDA^(⌢)|= 2m∠ABC; = 2 ⋅ 70^{∘}; = 140^{∘}.]

Now, we can find the measure of [MATH: \overset{\frown}{ABC}] as

[MATH: mABC^(⌢)|= 360^{∘} − mCDA^(⌢); = 360^{∘} − 140^{∘}; = 220^{∘}.]

Finally, we obtain [MATH: mBC^(⌢)|= mABC^(⌢) − mAB^(⌢); = 220^{∘} − 60^{∘}; = 160^{∘}.]

sections.readable_text:
In the diagram below, the length of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] equals [MATH: 10\pi] and [MATH: m\angle{BCA} = 50^\circ.] What is the radius of the circle?

[IMG: /graphics/fbb58ffe13a047697d6a1f5947ea5b3b]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
According to the inscribed angle theorem, the measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of its intercepted arc. Therefore,

[MATH: mAB^(⌢)|= 2m∠BCA; = 2 ⋅ 50^{∘}; = 100^{∘}.]

The corresponding central angle of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] is [MATH: \angle{AOB}.]

Notice that [MATH: \dfrac{m\angle{AOB}}{360^\circ} = \dfrac{100^\circ}{360^\circ} = \dfrac{5}{18}.]

Now, if the circumference of the circle is [MATH: C=2 \pi r], then we can write an equation for the length of the arc [MATH: \overset{\frown}{AB}] as follows:

[MATH: (5)/(18)C|= 10π; (5)/(18) ⋅ 2πr|= 10π; (5)/(9)πr|= 10π]

Solving for [MATH: r,] we get [MATH: (5)/(9)r|= 10; r|= (90)/(5); r|= 18.]
